implementation_notes: Kotlin inherits Java's cost profile — a JVM per service, with the startup and heap overhead multiplied by the count — and Ktor makes a lightweight server trivially easy, which is the accelerant. The Kotlin-specific sprawl form is a service per Kotlin module, so the build module boundary and the deploy boundary are the same thing by default; separating them (modules inside one deployment) is the consolidation and requires nothing but a decision. Coroutines also tempt the opposite mistake: concurrency inside a service added without a requirement, which is a per-service problem rather than a sprawl one but compounds the operational burden.
idiom_name: Ktor application per module; JVM service per domain
pitfalls: A service per Gradle module makes the module boundary and the deploy boundary identical by default; separating them is free and is the consolidation.
The JVM per service multiplies heap, GC and security-flag maintenance by the service count.
Ktor's zero-argument engine choice makes starting a new service a one-line decision with none of the ceremony that used to slow people down.
